  • Overall, it affirms Québec's autonomy from the federal government and creates new tools to defend it.
Part 1 Constitution of Québec
  • Creates a text that affirms Québec's primacy over any incompatible rule and defines the Québec nation.
  • Includes personal rights and freedoms and fundamental language rights.
  • Sets out the roles of Québec's legislative, executive and judicial branches.
  • Affirms values such as equality between women and men as founding principles.
Part 2 Act respecting Québec's constitutional autonomy
  • Creates a new law to guide the actions of the National Assembly and the government on Québec's autonomy.

  • Sets the rules for appointing its members and their term of office.
  • Allows the National Assembly's Office to adopt ethics rules for council members.
Part 4 Constitution Act, 1867
  • Removes rules about the former Legislative Council of Québec, which no longer exists.
  • Replaces the word "legislature" with "Parliament of Québec."
  • Adds state secularism, the model of integration into the Québec nation, and the civil law tradition as fundamental characteristics of Québec.

  • Specifies that the Civil Code applies in harmony with the new Constitution of Québec.
Part 6 Executive Power Act
  • Provides that the premier will designate a person to hold the position of Officer of Québec.
Part 7 Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms
  • Specifies that rights and freedoms must be interpreted in balance with the collective rights of the Québec nation.
  • Provides that in the event of a conflict, the right to equality between women and men takes precedence over freedom of religion.
Part 8 Code of Civil Procedure
  • Sets rules for requests to suspend the application of a law passed by the Parliament of Québec.
  • Prevents a court from raising a constitutional question on its own or forcing the parties to do so.
Part 9 Vocabulary changes

26993:
• This bill simplifies the rules that professional orders must follow to adopt their regulations.
  • It also allows more health professionals to perform acts they could not perform before.
Part 1 Professional Code
  • Professional orders can adopt certain regulations without the approval of the Office des professions or the government.
  • The Office des professions, not the government, must approve the orders' codes of ethics.
  • The Office can now decide on its own which diplomas are required to get a professional licence.
  • The Office must create a common rule for all orders to settle disputes over professionals' bills.
  • The Office can create a rule that applies to one or more orders at the same time, after consulting them.
  • The Office becomes solely responsible for ethics rules for members of orders' boards of directors, and can investigate and impose sanctions.
  • The public list of an order's members (the roll) will have to include more information.
  • The minimum number of signatures required to request a special general meeting of an order is changing.
  • Allows people with a psychotherapist permit obtained elsewhere in Canada to practise this profession in Québec.
Part 2 Act respecting nurses
  • Nurses will be able to start examinations and tests in more situations, not only in public health.
  • They will be able to prescribe examinations, tests, medications, other substances, products and dressings, according to rules to be set.
  • Removes the rule that reserved voting rights at general meetings to section delegates only.
Part 3 Midwives Act
  • Midwives will be able to prescribe and provide more types of contraception.
  • They will be able to screen more broadly for sexually transmitted and blood-borne infections.
  • They will be able to treat these infections in a person without symptoms if their test is positive.
Part 4 Optometry Act
  • Optometrists will be able to prescribe and provide more medications and offer more care than before.
Part 5 Act respecting dietitians-nutritionists
  • Their scope of practice is expanded and they will no longer need a medical prescription for certain reserved acts.
Part 6 Professional Code (psychotherapy)
  • Ends the activities of the Interdisciplinary Advisory Council on the Practice of Psychotherapy.
  • Marriage and family therapists will be able to practise psychotherapy without a specific permit, like psychologists and doctors.
  • The Office will be able to authorize students to perform certain psychotherapy acts during their training.
Part 7 Act respecting agrologists
  • An act performed by an agrologist will be considered practice of the profession even if it is not done for payment.
Part 8 Pharmacy Act
  • The government will be able to allow a pharmacist to prescribe or substitute a medication with another made by a company in which they have a financial interest, under specific conditions.
Part 9 Act respecting prescription drug insurance
  • A drug manufacturer will be able to pay certain benefits to an intermediary, such as a banner or pharmacy chain.
Part 10 Regulation respecting the conditions for recognition of a manufacturer and a wholesaler of medications
  • A manufacturer will also be able to pay these benefits to a drug wholesaler.
  • Several other professional acts (notaries, lawyers, land surveyors, denturologists, medical imaging technologists, etc.) receive technical adjustments to align with these changes.

• This bill changes the rules on collective agreement decrees and on work in the construction industry.
  • It also affects several sector-specific decrees (trucking, automobile services, building maintenance, etc.) through concordance adjustments.

  • The Minister of Labour now decides on his own about changes requested by a joint committee (which oversees the application of a decree) or a contracting party.

  • To prevent a decree from being renewed, an employer or union must notify the minister during the sixth month before the decree ends.
  • The minister must check that employer and union associations truly represent the people concerned before extending or changing a decree.
  • The minister can give directions to joint committees on their proper management, including for inspections.
  • The minister no longer has to publish notices in newspapers for a request to extend or change a decree.
  • Joint committees no longer have to send their budget forecasts and financial statements to the minister every year.
  • Joint committees no longer need to be recognized as training mutuals to help train workers and use subsidies for that purpose.

  • The Québec Cabinet will be able, without a new vote at the National Assembly, to set special labour standards for a trade or industry whose decree has expired.

  • Clarifies the working conditions of health and safety representatives on job sites.
Part 4 Act respecting labour relations... (construction)
  • Sets rules for adding or removing health and safety representatives or coordinators at the start and end of work on certain job sites.
  • The total cost of the work no longer counts in deciding whether these people must be designated.
  • A project owner must now notify the associations concerned when a full-time health and safety representative is required.
  • Work done by permanent employees of the Société des établissements de plein air du Québec, housing cooperatives or non-profit housing organizations is no longer covered by this act.
  • The Québec Cabinet will be able to launch pilot projects to test or improve the rules of this act.
  • The Commission de la construction du Québec will be able to create, through a rule without a new vote, an additional preventive withdrawal program for pregnant or breastfeeding workers, in addition to the existing program.

27679:
• The bill creates a new right allowing a person who is worried to obtain information about an intimate partner who may pose a risk to their safety.
  • It establishes a comprehensive process involving the Sûreté du Québec and a designated body to handle these requests and disclose the information.
  • New act respecting the disclosure of information: a person at risk, or someone acting on their behalf with their consent, may request information about their intimate partner.
  • New act: a minor aged 14 or over may submit such a request on their own.
  • New act: the government may, by regulation, designate other persons or categories of persons who may submit a request.
  • New act: police officers and workers from support organizations may inform a person at risk about the request process if it could benefit them.
  • New act: a police officer may, in these cases, disclose the identity of the partner who is the subject of a possible request.
  • New act: the Sûreté du Québec conducts the searches and transmits the relevant information to a body designated by the minister responsible for the status of women.
  • New act: a designated person, subject to regulatory conditions, meets with the person at risk to verbally communicate the information or the absence of relevant information.
  • New act: this person may also direct the person at risk to specialized resources and provide additional information.
  • New act: restrictions govern the disclosure to the intimate partner of the existence of a request and personal information concerning them.
  • New act: rules limit the further communication and use of the information obtained.
  • New act: certain persons benefit from immunity for acts performed in the exercise of their duties related to this process.
  • New act: these persons cannot be compelled to testify before a court concerning this information.
  • New act: penal offences are provided for breaches of the rules on communication or use of information.
  • Act respecting the Québec correctional system: revises the rules on disclosing to victims information concerning incarcerated persons or those under the supervision of correctional services.
  • Act respecting the Ministère de la Sécurité publique: consequential adjustments related to the creation of the new information disclosure regime.

27753:
• Creates a new office in the judicial system: the special clerk, who helps process cases before the courts.
  • Sets out how these people are chosen, appointed, paid and supervised in their work.
Part 1 Courts of Justice Act
  • Creates rules for the appointment, term and jurisdiction of special clerks across Québec.
  • Provides for a coordinating special clerk who oversees the work of other special clerks.
  • Allows a Québec Cabinet rule, without a new vote in the Assembly, on the recruitment and selection of special clerks.
  • Allows a Québec Cabinet rule, without a new vote in the Assembly, on their salary and benefits.
  • Sets ethics rules for special clerks and a process for handling complaints against them.
  • Spells out the duties and powers that special clerks may exercise in court cases.
Part 2 Code of Civil Procedure
  • Adjusts procedural rules to reflect the powers of special clerks.
Part 3 Youth Protection Act
  • Adapts certain rules to allow special clerks to step in on relevant cases.
Part 4 Act respecting the civil aspects of international and interprovincial child abduction
  • Adjusts related rules to match the special clerk changes.
  • Cities and Towns Act, Municipal Code of Québec, Forest Credit Act, Act respecting the Department of Justice, Act respecting the Executive Council, Act respecting the method of payment for electricity and gas services, Education Act for Cree, Inuit and Naskapi Native Persons: technical adjustments to match the new office of special clerk.
Part 5 Code of ethics of advocates, Code of ethics of notaries, and regulations on the selection of chairs of disciplinary councils and judges
  • Technical adjustments to match this reform.
